phrases.translation: Those who disbelieve and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah,
phrases.explanation: The surah opens by naming two things the disbelievers do together. They deny the oneness of God and worship something besides Him, and they also turn others away from the way of Islam. The verse pairs the two because the one who has left the road can block it for those behind him. Their opposition is not private, since the harm reaches whoever they can turn aside.

phrases.translation: He will render their deeds void
phrases.explanation: The outcome is stated at once. God causes their works to come to nothing, and the emptiness is explained as loss of guidance and of a straight path. Their deeds were not good deeds spoiled, but works performed along the way of the enemy of God rather than along the straight road. The verse says what becomes of labour spent in the wrong direction, and the rest of the surah works out the contrast.

phrases.translation: As for those who believe, do good, and have faith in what has been revealed to Muḥammad—which is the truth from their Lord—
phrases.explanation: The opposite case is set beside the first. Those who believe, do good and hold true what was sent down to Muhammad, which is the truth from their Lord, are described by faith, action and acceptance at once. The verse names the revelation as truth from their Lord, since the acceptance rests on where it came from. One report ties this verse to the believers of Medina while the previous one concerns the people of Mecca.

phrases.translation: He will absolve them of their sins and improve their condition
phrases.explanation: Their reward is given in two parts. God wipes out the evil they committed, so that He neither calls them to account for it nor punishes them, and He sets their condition right. The righting covers their affairs in this world among those close to Him and their inheritance of lasting felicity in the gardens of the next. The verse replaces the voiding of deeds with remission and repair, and the two belong to the same reckoning.

phrases.translation: This is because the disbelievers follow falsehood, while the believers follow the truth from their Lord.
phrases.explanation: The verse gives the reason for the two outcomes. The disbelievers follow falsehood, which one report names plainly as Satan, and they obey him. The believers follow the truth that came from their Lord, and that is the Prophet and what he brought of light and proof. The differing destinies of the previous verses are traced back to the differing things each group followed.

phrases.translation: This is how Allah shows people their true state ˹of faith˺
phrases.explanation: The statement then widens into a principle. Just as God has dealt with the group of belief and the group of disbelief, so does He set out parables for people and make them vivid. The purpose is that each person sees his own case described and recognises where he stands. The verse closes the opening passage by turning a report about two groups into a lesson addressed to everyone who hears it.

phrases.translation: So when you meet the disbelievers ˹in battle˺, strike ˹their˺ necks until you have thoroughly subdued them,
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to fighting. The believers are told to strike the necks of those who deny God when they meet them in battle, and to keep at it until the enemy has been subdued. The pairing of the two words shows that the aim is to end the resistance, not to prolong it. The command is given to a community that had been enduring harm, and it is stated in the plain language of the field.

phrases.translation: then bind them firmly. Later ˹free them either as˺ an act of grace or by ransom until the war comes to an end.
phrases.explanation: Once the enemy is overcome and taken captive, the bonds are to be made firm. The captives are then to be released either as a favour without payment or against a ransom, and this arrangement lasts until the war puts down its burdens. One reading of that phrase takes it as the end of fighting through the enemy's acceptance of Islam. The verse therefore sets limits on the treatment of those who have been captured.

phrases.translation: So will it be. Had Allah willed, He ˹Himself˺ could have inflicted punishment on them. But He does ˹this only to˺ test some of you by means of others.
phrases.explanation: Had God willed, He could have taken vengeance on the enemy Himself, and the fighting was ordained so that some believers would be tested by means of others. The reports differ over whether the choice between release, ransom and killing remains open or was later narrowed, and the stronger view is that this verse stands unaltered. What the Prophet did in his own campaigns is cited as the working example.

phrases.translation: And those who are martyred in the cause of Allah, He will never render their deeds void
phrases.explanation: The passage closes with a promise for those who die in the fighting. God will never let their deeds be lost, and the following verse begins to say what He will give them instead. The words are read by the reciters in several forms, as those who fought, those who were killed, and those killed in turn, and the form naming those who fought is preferred. One report ties the verse to the day of Uḥud, when the fighting had taken its toll.

phrases.translation: He will guide them ˹to their reward˺,
phrases.explanation: The promise made at the end of the previous verse continues. God will guide those who fought to what pleases Him and what He loves, and the guidance is given after death as a gift rather than as a lesson, since the reward is being described. The verse opens the account of what awaits them with the road itself, before it says anything about their state.

phrases.translation: improve their condition
phrases.explanation: The second half of the promise is the righting of their condition. Their affair is set in order in this world among those close to God, and in the next by their inheriting lasting felicity and dwelling forever in His gardens. Guidance and repair are given together, since the road and the state are both gifts. The verse leaves nothing of the fighters' future outside God's care.

phrases.translation: and admit them into Paradise, having made it known to them
phrases.explanation: The reward is completed with entry into Paradise. The word describing it as made known is explained in several ways, all pointing to familiarity: the people of the Garden will know the way to their dwellings there as they knew the way home in this world, or better. One report describes them being held on a bridge between the Garden and the Fire until wrongs among them are settled, and then admitted. The closeness of the place is the point of the promise.

phrases.translation: O believers! If you stand up for Allah,
phrases.explanation: The address turns to the believers with a condition. If they help God, meaning if they aid His Messenger against His enemies and fight alongside him so that His word is raised, then He will help them against those enemies and give them victory. One report calls this a right that God has bound Himself to, that He helps whoever helps Him. The verse makes the help mutual in wording while leaving the power entirely with God.

phrases.translation: He will help you and make your steps firm
phrases.explanation: The second half of the promise is steadiness. God will strengthen them and plant courage in them, so that they do not turn away even when the enemy is many and they are few. Firm feet are the image of a line that holds its ground. The verse closes by naming the practical effect of divine help, which is not only victory but the ability to stand until it comes.

phrases.translation: As for the disbelievers, may they be doomed
phrases.explanation: The disbelievers are then named with a curse. Perdition is upon them, and the word is explained as humiliation, misery and calamity. The expression has the force of a supplication, which is why the next clause follows it as though it were a statement. The verse sets the state of the deniers beside the firm steps promised to the believers in the verse before.

phrases.translation: and may He render their deeds void
phrases.explanation: Their works are made void, and the emptiness is described as deeds performed without guidance and without rightness. The reason given is that they were done in obedience to the devil rather than to the Most Merciful. One report adds that this is the misguidance God has told of, that He leads astray whom He wills. The sentence repeats the opening of the surah, now with the cause attached to it.

phrases.translation: That is because they detest what Allah has revealed,
phrases.explanation: The reason for their ruin is stated. They detested the Book God sent down to His Prophet, loathed it and denied it, and called it manifest sorcery. The verse names the motive as hatred rather than doubt, which explains why the punishment is described as misery rather than correction. What they rejected was not a claim they had examined and found wanting.

phrases.translation: so He has rendered their deeds void
phrases.explanation: The consequence follows the motive. God has undone the deeds they performed in the world, and those deeds are identified as the worship of idols, which profited them in neither life and became the cause of their burning. One report says this judgement covers every community that does not believe in God. The verse closes the opening movement of the surah by naming both the offence and its cost.

phrases.translation: Have they not travelled throughout the land to see what was the end of those before them?
phrases.explanation: The verse asks why the deniers have not looked at the road they travel. Their journeys took them to Syria, where they could see what became of the people of the rock and of Thamud, and to Yemen, where they could see what became of Sheba. The question is a rebuke rather than a request for information, since the ruins were within reach of their trade. The evidence was not hidden from them, only unexamined.

phrases.translation: Allah annihilated them, and a similar fate awaits the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: The answer to the question is supplied. God destroyed those earlier communities for denying their messengers and rejecting their counsel, and He laid their dwellings waste over them. The verse then states that the same end awaits the disbelievers of Quraysh if they persist, and one report calls this a threat of immediate punishment. The past is offered as a warning, and the warning is that the pattern does not change.

phrases.translation: This is because Allah is the Patron of the believers
phrases.explanation: The verse names the reason for the two outcomes. What God did with the believers, aiding them and making their feet firm, and with the disbelievers, destroying them, follows from this: God is the patron of those who believe in Him and obey His messenger. The word means a protector who takes the affair of his client in hand. One early reading brings the particle out more plainly as a statement of exclusive patronage.

phrases.translation: while the disbelievers have no patron
phrases.explanation: The other half of the contrast is stated in the negative. The disbelievers have no patron and no helper in God. The idols they counted on are not named here, since the point is the absence itself. With the patronage on one side and the void on the other, the differing ends described in the previous verses are accounted for.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah will admit those who believe and do good into Gardens under which rivers flow.
phrases.explanation: The believers are given their destination. God will admit those who believe and do good into gardens beneath whose trees the rivers run, and the verse calls this an honouring of their faith in Him and in His messenger. Faith and action are named together again, as they were at the opening of the surah. The reward is stated as an act of God rather than a wage earned.

phrases.translation: As for the disbelievers, they enjoy themselves and feed like cattle. But the Fire will be their home
phrases.explanation: The disbelievers are described in a single image. They enjoy the passing goods of this world, its adornment and its excess, and they eat without reflecting on the return or learning from the proofs. Their likeness is the cattle, which know nothing beyond grazing. The verse adds that the Fire is their dwelling and their refuge, and that they return to it after death. The comparison measures them by what they think about, not by what they own.

phrases.translation: ˹Imagine, O Prophet,˺ how many societies We destroyed that were far superior in might than your society—which drove you out—
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is given a comparison drawn from the towns of the past. Many a town was stronger than Mecca, the town whose people drove him out, with harsher violence, greater numbers and better equipment. God destroyed them all, and the verse notes that their strength did not save them when the decree came. One report ties the verse to the Prophet's words on leaving Mecca, when he named it the dearest land to him and to God.

phrases.translation: and there was none to help them
phrases.explanation: The last clause denies them any support. There was no helper for them, either at the time of their destruction or now, against the punishment of God. The grammar of the sentence is discussed, and the sense is the same on either account. The verse leaves the people of Mecca to draw the conclusion about their own town, since the greater ones before it found no one to stand with them.

phrases.translation: Can those ˹believers˺ who stand on clear proof from their Lord be like those whose evil deeds are made appealing to them
phrases.explanation: The question asks whether two people can be alike. The first stands on a clear proof from his Lord, a ground of evidence and a plain declaration, so that he worships with insight and knows that obedience is rewarded and disobedience punished. The verse does not describe the second yet, it only asks whether the two are equal. One report identifies the first as the Prophet himself.

phrases.translation: and ˹only˺ follow their desires
phrases.explanation: The second person is described by what has happened to him. The evil of his deeds has been made beautiful in his eyes by Satan, so that he goes on doing them, and he follows what his own soul calls him to of disobedience and idol worship. He has no proof for any of it. The verse completes the comparison by showing that one of the two has evidence and the other only appetite, which answers the question it asked.

phrases.translation: The description of the Paradise promised to the righteous is that in it are rivers of fresh water,
phrases.explanation: The Garden is described by what flows through it. The first river is water that never spoils, meaning water whose smell has not changed and turned foul. The word chosen carries the idea of standing water that has gone bad, and the verse denies that anything of the kind can happen there. The promise is stated in the concrete terms of a dry land where water is the first thing people think of.

phrases.translation: rivers of milk that never changes in taste,
phrases.explanation: Milk is added to the rivers. Its taste does not change, and the explanation given is that it was never drawn from an animal, since milk alters when it leaves the udder. It was created in the rivers from the beginning and stays as it was made. The same point holds for the other rivers, that what flows there is made directly and needs no process to keep it sweet.

phrases.translation: rivers of wine delicious to drink, and rivers of pure honey.
phrases.explanation: The third river is wine, described as a delight to those who drink it. The word for delight is read in the genitive by the reciters, describing the wine itself, and the other cases are grammatically possible but not transmitted. One report says no Magian trodden it, no Satan blown into it and no sun harmed it. The drink that causes harm and quarrel in this world is promised there as pure pleasure.

phrases.translation: There they will ˹also˺ have all kinds of fruit, and forgiveness from their Lord.
phrases.explanation: The fourth river is honey, and it is called purified, meaning free of the dregs that honey of this world carries until it is strained. The verse then adds all kinds of fruit and forgiveness from their Lord, so that the list ends not with food but with the remission of sins. Forgiveness is placed last because it is the greatest of the gifts named, and the one the others depend on.

phrases.translation: ˹Can they be˺ like those who will stay in the Fire forever, left to drink boiling water that will tear apart their insides
phrases.explanation: The question sets the two ends side by side. Is the one who enjoys this like the one who stays in the Fire forever and is given boiling water that tears apart his insides? The verse leaves the answer unspoken, since the hearer supplies it. The water of this world appears in both halves, cool and unspoiled in one, scalding and destructive in the other.

phrases.translation: There are some of them who listen to you ˹O Prophet˺, but when they depart from you, they say ˹mockingly˺ to those ˹believers˺ gifted with knowledge,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes a listener who takes nothing in. Such a person hears what the Prophet says but does not keep it or understand it, and the reason given is disdain for the recitation and indifference to the call. The hearing is physical only, since the ear is present and the heart is not. The verse names these people among the deniers, and other reports identify them as the hypocrites.

phrases.translation: “What did he just say?”
phrases.explanation: Once out of the gathering they turn to those who were given knowledge and ask what was said. The question is not the request of a learner, it is a way of showing that they paid no attention and set no value on the words. One report says the questioners were themselves asked, and that a Companion counted himself among those who were asked. The mockery is aimed at the speaker as much as at the message.

phrases.translation: These are the ones whose hearts Allah has sealed and who ˹only˺ follow their desires
phrases.explanation: The verse then gives the reason for their condition. God has sealed their hearts, so that they are not guided to the truth sent with His messenger, and they follow what their own souls call them to. The passage makes the same judgement on them as on the idolaters, since both have abandoned the religion and taken their desires as a guide. The sealing is stated as the consequence of that choice, not as a barrier placed before it.

phrases.translation: As for those who are ˹rightly˺ guided,
phrases.explanation: The verse turns from the sealed hearts to their opposite. Those whom God has helped to follow the truth, and whose hearts He opened to belief in Him and in His messenger, are given more than they had. The contrast with the previous verse is exact: one group hears and asks what was said, the other hears and gains.

phrases.translation: He increases them in guidance and blesses them with righteousness
phrases.explanation: The increase is described. When the Prophet recited, the hypocrites asked what he had said, while God increased the guided among them in faith upon their faith and in clarity upon clarity. One report adds that the abrogating and the abrogated verses increased them in guidance, since understanding how the revelation fits together deepened their certainty. The verse also says God gave them their God-fearingness, meaning He brought them to act on it.

phrases.translation: Are they only waiting for the Hour to take them by surprise?
phrases.explanation: The question names what the deniers are waiting for. They await nothing but the Hour, which will come on them suddenly without warning, and their waiting is the waiting of those who do not expect it to arrive. The verse is addressed to the people of denial and hypocrisy together, and it asks what else they could be expecting. The answer implied is that there is nothing left to wait for but the event itself.

phrases.translation: Yet ˹some of˺ its signs have already come.
phrases.explanation: The portents have already come. The word is explained as the signs and harbingers of the Hour, and one report says the Hour has drawn near and the term of the servants has come close. The verse therefore tells the deniers that the warning has already begun, and that waiting for a further proof is a delay they cannot justify. The signs are named without a list, since the hearers are expected to know what has reached them.

phrases.translation: Once it actually befalls them, will it not be too late to be mindful
phrases.explanation: The last clause asks what good their remembering will do once the Hour has come. When it arrives it is a time of recompense, not a time for seeking forgiveness or showing repentance, so the reminder that would have helped them earlier is no longer of use. The verse closes the passage with a question rather than a statement, and the answer is left to the hearer. The point is not that memory fails but that the moment for it has passed.

phrases.translation: So, know ˹well, O Prophet,˺ that there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Allah.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to know, not merely to hear. There is no god worthy of worship but God, the Creator and Owner of all things, to whom everything beneath Him submits. The command is put in the form of knowledge because the matter is settled and no argument remains. He is addressed directly here, which gives the verse its intimate tone after the long account of the hypocrites.

phrases.translation: And seek forgiveness for your shortcomings and for ˹the sins of˺ the believing men and women.
phrases.explanation: The command then turns to seeking forgiveness, for his own shortcomings past and new and for the believing men and women. The Prophet is included among those who ask, and his asking is joined to asking for the whole community. One report has a Companion marvel that the Prophet sought forgiveness for them, and the Prophet answered that it was so and recited this verse. The verse makes intercession for the believers a continuing duty.

phrases.translation: For Allah ˹fully˺ knows your movements and places of rest ˹O people˺
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with God's knowledge of movement and rest. He knows what people occupy themselves with while awake and where they settle when they sleep, and nothing of it is hidden from Him, and He will requite them for it. The two words cover the whole of a day, so the verse leaves no part of life outside the account. Knowledge here is the ground of the command to seek forgiveness.

phrases.translation: And the believers say, “If only a sûrah was revealed ˹allowing self-defence˺!”
phrases.explanation: The believers are described asking for a chapter that would permit fighting. Their wish is for the command that would let them answer the harm they were suffering, and it is a wish for permission rather than for war. The verse puts their eagerness in the plainest terms before showing what the same command does to others. The two responses to one revelation divide the community.

phrases.translation: Yet when a precise sûrah is revealed, in which fighting is ˹explicitly˺ mentioned, you see those with sickness in their hearts staring at you like someone in the throes of death.
phrases.explanation: When a clear chapter comes down with fighting named in it, the reaction is visible. Those with sickness in their hearts look at the Prophet like a man in the throes of death, out of fear that they will be sent out and commanded to fight. One report says every chapter mentioning fighting is the heaviest part of the Qur'an for the hypocrites. The verse describes the look rather than the words, since the fear shows before it speaks.

phrases.translation: It would have been better for them
phrases.explanation: The sentence that follows is a short condemnation. Better for them would have been the obedience and the fitting word that the next verse names. The clause is left without its verb at the end of the verse, so that the reader turns the page to learn what was better. The pause is deliberate, and the next verse supplies the answer the verse withholds.

phrases.translation: to obey and speak rightly.
phrases.explanation: Obedience and a right word are named as what would have been better for them. The two cover the act and the speech, since the hypocrite fails in both, refusing the command and answering with words that do not fit. The verse supplies the completion of the sentence left open before it. What was wanted was not courage in battle first, but a truthful reply when the command came.

phrases.translation: Then when fighting was ordained, it surely would have been better for them if they were true to Allah
phrases.explanation: Then the command to fight was given, and the verse says what would have profited them at that point. Had they been true to God, keeping faith with Him and speaking honestly, it would have been better for them than the evasion they chose. Truthfulness to God is set against the looking away described earlier. The verse ends the passage on the hypocrites by naming the one thing that would have saved them.

phrases.translation: Now if you ˹hypocrites˺ turn away,
phrases.explanation: The question is put to those who looked away when fighting was named. If they turn away from what God has sent down and part with the rulings of His Book, what is to be expected of them? The verse does not ask about a future they cannot know, it asks about the direction they are already taking. Turning back from the revelation is presented as the beginning of a road.

phrases.translation: perhaps you would then spread corruption throughout the land and sever your ˹ties of˺ kinship
phrases.explanation: The end of that road is named. They would spread corruption in the land, shedding blood and returning to the division they had before Islam, and they would sever the ties of kinship after God had united their hearts. One report says they did exactly this when they turned from the Book. The verse measures their evasion against the peace that the revelation had brought them, and the choice is set before them in those terms.

phrases.translation: These are the ones who Allah has condemned,
phrases.explanation: The verse names those who do these things as the ones God has cursed, meaning He has driven them far from His mercy. The curse is stated first and the effects follow. The description is not of a punishment in the next life only, since what is described next happens to them in this world as well. Their own conduct and their condition are joined in the sentence.

phrases.translation: deafening them and blinding their eyes
phrases.explanation: The curse is described in two acts. God has made them deaf, so that they take nothing from the admonitions of His revelation, and He has blinded their eyes, so that they no longer discern His proofs or remember the signs they see. The deafness and blindness are of the understanding rather than the ear and the eye. The verse leaves them with faculties intact and the use of them gone.

phrases.translation: Do they not then reflect on the Quran?
phrases.explanation: The question asks why the hypocrites do not think about the verses that admonish them. If they pondered the Qur'an and the proofs made clear in it, they would see the error of what they persist in and turn from it. One report says they would find in the Book what would restrain them from disobedience if people would understand it. The verse puts reflection forward as the missing step, not the evidence.

phrases.translation: Or are there locks upon their hearts
phrases.explanation: The second half offers the alternative explanation. Perhaps there are locks on their hearts, so that nothing enters and the admonitions cannot reach them. The image is of a door barred from the inside, and it answers the first question by naming the reason for the failure. One report tells of a young man from Yemen who answered the verse by saying that the locks are indeed there until God opens them.

phrases.translation: Indeed, those who relapse ˹into disbelief˺ after ˹true˺ guidance has become clear to them,
phrases.explanation: The verse names those who turn back after the guidance has become clear. They knew the proof and then preferred error to guidance, and the turning is deliberate because the clarity came first. Reports differ over who is meant, with the People of the Book named by one and the hypocrites by another. The verse keeps its force either way, since it describes a relapse made in full knowledge.

phrases.translation: ˹it is˺ Satan ˹that˺ has tempted them, luring them with false hopes
phrases.explanation: The cause of the relapse is named as Satan, who made the turn appear good to them and drew them on with false hopes. The deception is described as prolonged, since God granted them time and they mistook the delay for approval. One set of readings gives the verb as God granting the respite and another as the deception being done to them, and the meanings lie close together. The verse leaves the two acts side by side, the tempting and the time allowed.

phrases.translation: That is because they said ˹privately˺ to those who ˹also˺ detest what Allah has revealed, “We will obey you in some matters.”
phrases.explanation: The verse gives the reason for the relapse. The hypocrites spoke privately to those who hated what God had sent down, meaning the command to fight, and promised to obey them in part of the matter. The obedience promised was obedience against God and His messenger, and it was given in secret because it could not be defended in the open. The verse records the bargain that turned them back.

phrases.translation: But Allah ˹fully˺ knows what they are hiding
phrases.explanation: The secret is not secret. God knows what they conceal, and the verse notes that the counsel of those two parties does not remain hidden from Him, nor does anything else. The word for what they hide is read as a plural and as a verbal noun, and both readings are accepted. The sentence closes the account of the conspiracy by placing it in full view of the One who will judge it.

phrases.translation: Then how ˹horrible˺ will it be when the angels take their souls,
phrases.explanation: The question turns from their secrecy to their end. If God knows what they hide, how will it be when the angels take their souls at death? The verse answers its own question by describing the moment, which is not hidden from God either. The scene is the point at which the concealment stops being possible.

phrases.translation: beating their faces and backs
phrases.explanation: The angels strike their faces and their backs as they take them, and the word for backs is explained as their backsides. The blows fall on the front and the back at once, so that there is nowhere to turn. The verse names no dialogue and no defence, only the seizure. The next verse gives the reason for it, which is what they followed and what they hated.

phrases.translation: This is because they follow whatever displeases Allah and hate whatever pleases Him,
phrases.explanation: The reason for the blows is stated. They followed what angered God, which one report identifies as obedience to Satan, and they detested what would have pleased Him, which is the fighting He had made obligatory on them. The two halves describe a person who chose the thing forbidden and resented the thing commanded. The verse explains the treatment they receive at death as the fruit of that choice.

phrases.translation: so He has rendered their deeds void
phrases.explanation: The consequence is the nullifying of their works. God made the reward of what they did void and caused it to vanish, because the deeds were done for something other than His pleasure and love. The works were not few but misdirected, and so they profited no one. The verse closes the passage on the hypocrites with the same verdict the surah pronounced at its opening over the disbelievers.

phrases.translation: Or do those with sickness in their hearts think that Allah will not ˹be able to˺ expose their malice
phrases.explanation: The question is put to those with sickness in their hearts, meaning doubt about their religion and weakness of conviction. Do they suppose that God will never bring their rancour toward the believers into the open? The verse names the malice they carry and asks whether they think it can stay hidden. The next verse answers by saying that God could show them to the Prophet by their marks, and that he will know them by their tone of speech.

phrases.translation: Had We willed, We could have truly shown them to you ˹O Prophet˺, and you would have certainly recognized them by their appearance.
phrases.explanation: The answer to the previous question begins with a conditional. Had God willed, He could have shown the hypocrites to the Prophet directly, so that he would know them by their marks, the signs of hypocrisy visible in the drift of their words and the look of their deeds. The verse places that power with God and does not say it was withheld out of weakness. What follows explains how they would in fact be known.

phrases.translation: But you will surely recognize them by their tone of speech.
phrases.explanation: The recognition is promised by another route. The Prophet will know them by their tone of speech, which one report explains as the import of their words. The verse does not describe a secret sign but the way a person's speech betrays what he carries, and one report notes that God made them known to him in the chapter of repentance, where their treatment is set out. The knowledge is certain even when the identity is not displayed.

phrases.translation: And Allah ˹fully˺ knows your doings ˹O people˺
phrases.explanation: The verse closes by turning to the hearers. God knows their deeds, and nothing of obedience or deviation is hidden from Him, and He will requite each person for it. The clause widens the address from the hypocrites to everyone listening, so that no one supposes himself outside the account. The disclosure of hidden malice is thus part of a knowledge that covers every deed.

phrases.translation: We will certainly test you ˹believers˺ until We prove those of you who ˹truly˺ struggle ˹in Allah’s cause˺ and remain steadfast,
phrases.explanation: The believers are told plainly that they will be tested, and the testing is named as fighting and struggle against the enemies of God. The purpose given is that those who struggle and those who are patient become known and are distinguished from the doubters and the hypocrites. The verse speaks of God knowing, which here means making the distinction visible in the world. One report calls this world the abode of trial and points to the prophets who were tested before.

phrases.translation: and reveal how you conduct yourselves
phrases.explanation: The last clause adds a second kind of test. God will test what they report and say, so that the truthful is separated from the liar. The struggle tries the hand and the report tries the tongue, and the verse includes both. The reciters differ over whether the verbs are in the first person or the third, and the first person is preferred by consensus. The verse closes the passage by naming the two places where a person is found out.

phrases.translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve, hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah, and defy the Messenger after ˹true˺ guidance has become clear to them;
phrases.explanation: The verse names the full offence in one sentence. They disbelieve, they turn others away from the way of God, and they oppose the messenger after the guidance has become clear to them. The last clause removes the excuse of ignorance, since they knew he was a sent prophet and still fought him and harmed him. Their opposition is not against an idea they never understood.

phrases.translation: they will not harm Allah in the least, but He will render their deeds void
phrases.explanation: The harm they intend does not reach God. He carries out His command, helps His messenger and makes him victorious over those who oppose him, so their resistance changes nothing in His purpose. Their deeds, however, are nullified, and they will avail them in neither world. The verse measures the two sides of the struggle and shows which one is actually at risk.

phrases.translation: O believers! Obey Allah and obey the Messenger,
phrases.explanation: The believers are addressed directly. They are to obey God and obey the messenger in what both command and forbid, and the repetition of the verb gives the messenger's obedience the same weight as God's. The verse places the community under a single authority at the moment when the fighting has been ordained. Obedience is named before the warning that follows it.

phrases.translation: and do not let your deeds be in vain
phrases.explanation: The warning is against making their deeds void. Disobedience and disbelief can cancel the reward of good work already done, and the verse tells them not to let that happen. One report says that whoever is able should not let a good deed be erased by an evil one, since the good lifts away the evil and the evil lifts away the good. The verse closes by putting the responsibility for the loss on the one who acts.

phrases.translation: Surely those who disbelieve, hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah, and then die as disbelievers;
phrases.explanation: The verse returns to those who disbelieve and block the way of God. They deny His oneness, turn people from the religion with which He sent His messengers, and then die while still in that denial. The three clauses build a life that ends where it began, with the refusal intact. The verse names the end first because everything before it is measured by where it finished.

phrases.translation: Allah will never forgive them
phrases.explanation: The sentence follows: God will never forgive them. The unforgivable thing is not a doubt of the moment but a denial that lasted to the end of life, and the verse states the verdict in the strongest form the language allows. What they committed is not passed over but punished, and they are disgraced thereby in the sight of witnesses. The verse closes the matter with no further condition attached.

phrases.translation: So do not falter or cry for peace,
phrases.explanation: The believers are told not to weaken in the struggle and not to call for peace while they hold the advantage. The verse does not forbid peace in itself but forbids asking for it out of fear when they are the stronger party. One report says the words applied at a time when there were pacts and a truce, before fighting was commanded, and that the command to fight later settled the matter. The tone is encouragement rather than rebuke.

phrases.translation: for you will have the upper hand and Allah is with you.
phrases.explanation: The reason given is that they are the upper party and God is with them. One report explains the upper hand as being nearer to God than the enemy, and another as being the victors in the end even if they are overcome in some battles. God's being with them means His help against them. The verse supplies the ground for refusing a truce asked out of weakness.

phrases.translation: And He will never let your deeds go to waste
phrases.explanation: The last clause promises that nothing they do will be lost. God will not withhold the reward of their deeds or diminish the recompense for them, and the word carries the sense of being cheated of what is due. The promise answers the fear that sacrifice in the fighting might go unrewarded. The verse closes with an assurance that the account is kept in full.

phrases.translation: This worldly life is no more than play and amusement.
phrases.explanation: The verse names what the world actually is. The life of this world is play and amusement, and the passage is urging the believers to fight and to spend, so the point is that the love of a passing thing must not hold them back. Whatever falls outside the work done for God is play that fades, or a sin whose disgrace remains. The exception is what is done in His way and for His pleasure.

phrases.translation: But if you are faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, He will grant you your ˹full˺ reward, and will not ask you ˹to donate all˺ your wealth
phrases.explanation: The condition follows. If they believe and fear God by keeping His obligations and avoiding disobedience, He will give them their full reward, which is what remains of their life and is not nullified by the passing of the amusement. One reading of the last clause says God does not ask them for their wealth at all, only for the acknowledgement of His oneness and the devotion of obedience to Him. The verse sets the smallness of the ask against the size of the reward.

phrases.translation: If He were to do so and pressure you, you would withhold and He would bring out your resentment
phrases.explanation: God does not ask for the wealth because He knows what such an asking would do. If He demanded it and pressed the demand to the limit, they would be stingy and hold it back, and the resentment they carry would come out into the open. The word for pressing is explained as taking everything away with both hands. He knew that of them, and the meanness of their souls, and so He asked only for acknowledgement and obedience.

phrases.translation: Here you are, being invited to donate ˹a little˺ in the cause of Allah. Still some of you withhold.
phrases.explanation: The believers are addressed as people who are called to spend in the way of God, in the fighting and in support of His religion, and among them are those who hold back. The verse opens with the word that draws attention, a form that brings the matter close to the hearer. The call and the reluctance are named in the same sentence, so that the contrast is visible at once.

phrases.translation: And whoever does so, it is only to their own loss. For Allah is the Self-Sufficient, whereas you stand in need ˹of Him˺.
phrases.explanation: The miser is told who loses by it. Whoever withholds is only miserly toward himself, since a generous soul would not have held back. The verse then states the relation on which the whole appeal rests: God is self-sufficient and they are the needy. He has no need of their wealth or their spending, and the command was given so that they might reach the reward. The loss in withholding falls entirely on the one who withholds.

phrases.translation: If you ˹still˺ turn away, He will replace you with another people.
phrases.explanation: The verse then warns that the community is replaceable. If they turn away from the religion Muhammad brought, God will cause them to pass and bring another people in their place who will believe in it and act on it. One report says the Prophet struck the shoulder of Salman and named him and his people, and another report names the people of Yemen. The warning is directed at the community as a whole, not at any individual.

phrases.translation: And they will not be like you
phrases.explanation: The last clause describes the replacement. Those who come after will not be like the ones who turned away, since they will not be miserly with what they are commanded to spend and will not neglect the limits of their religion. The verse ends the surah on a promise and a threat at once, and it leaves the hearers to decide which description they want to be found under.
